details:
**"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth"**
The famous opening verse of Genesis, the first book of the Bible and the Torah. Its Hebrew name, Bereshit, means "in the beginning." Chapter 1 describes creation in six days, with God saying "Let there be light," repeating that "God saw that it was good," and commanding humans to "be fruitful and multiply."

**Adam and Eve and the Garden of Eden**
The first humans. Adam names the animals, and the serpent tempts Eve, who along with Adam eats fruit from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. They are expelled from Eden, whose entrance is then guarded by cherubim and a flaming sword.

**Cain and Abel**
The sons of Adam and Eve. Cain murders Abel and, when God asks where Abel is, replies "Am I my brother's keeper?" Cain is cursed and sent to wander in the Land of Nod, and Adam and Eve later have another son, Seth.

**Jacob and Esau**
The twin sons of Isaac and Rebekah, who is told "two nations are in thy womb." Esau is born red and hairy, with Jacob grasping his heel. Jacob buys Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew (pottage) and later tricks their blind father into blessing him by wearing goatskins to imitate Esau's hairy arms.

**Noah's flood**
God floods the earth, sparing only Noah's family and the animals on the ark. A dove returning with an olive branch signals that the waters have receded, and God sends a rainbow as a sign of his covenant never to destroy the earth by flood again.

**Jacob's ladder**
Jacob's dream at Bethel of a ladder (or stairway) reaching from earth to heaven, with angels going up and down it, during which God renews the covenant made with Abraham.

**Abraham's covenant and the birth of Isaac**
God makes a covenant with Abram, renames him Abraham, and promises his descendants the land "from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates." His elderly wife Sarah, renamed from Sarai, miraculously gives birth to Isaac.

**Hagar and Ishmael**
Because Sarah could not conceive, she gave her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abraham, and Hagar bore Ishmael. After Isaac's birth, Hagar and Ishmael are cast out into the wilderness. Ishmael is regarded as an ancestor of the Arabs.

**Sodom and Gomorrah and Lot's wife**
Abraham bargains with God, who agrees to spare Sodom if even ten righteous men can be found there, but they cannot. Two angels rescue Lot's family, and Lot's wife is turned into a pillar of salt for looking back at the destruction. Lot's daughters later bear his sons Moab and Ben-Ammi, ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

**Joseph and Potiphar**
Jacob's favorite son, sold into slavery in Egypt by his jealous brothers and bought by Potiphar. In prison he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, then interprets Pharaoh's dreams to predict seven years of plenty and seven of famine, rising to power under the Egyptian name Zaphnath-Paaneah. Genesis ends with Joseph forgiving his brothers and dying at age 110.

**Jacob, Laban, Rachel, and Leah**
Jacob works fourteen years for his uncle Laban to marry Laban's two daughters, Leah and Rachel. He also has children by their maids Bilhah and Zilpah, producing the twelve sons who become the tribes of Israel (including Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Dan). Jacob multiplies his own share of Laban's flocks by setting peeled branches of poplar and other trees before the animals.

**Jacob wrestling with the angel**
Jacob wrestles all night with a mysterious divine being, who cannot defeat him and touches the hollow of his thigh, dislocating his hip. Jacob is then renamed Israel.

**The curse of Ham**
After the flood, Noah plants a vineyard and gets drunk. His son Ham sees his nakedness, while his other sons Shem and Japheth cover him, so Noah curses Ham's son Canaan.

**Wife-sister stories with Abimelech of Gerar**
Twice in Genesis a patriarch passes his wife off as his sister to protect himself: Abraham with Sarah before Abimelech, king of Gerar, and later Isaac with Rebekah. Abraham and Abimelech later swear a treaty at Beersheba.

**Melchizedek**
The priest-king of Salem, "priest of the most high God," who blesses Abram with bread and wine after Abram rescues his nephew Lot from a coalition of kings that included the king of Shinar.
